Lecture 1- First Day Intro

This section of the course is about the movement of data from one machine to another.

All of the machines must agree on 'how' to send and receive this data. Machines agree by using well-defined protocols.

A protocol is a set of rules that gives meaning to the data that is transmitted across a network.

Data is raw and unstructured: 01010100

Information has meaning:

First Name: Mark

Usually, only the source and destination machines (or applications running on them) attempt to treat the data as information.

A network is a system of interconnected computers that can share data, and possibly information, with each other.

In computer systems, data comes in the form of bits. Either 1's or 0's. All data that goes across a network is in this form.

Data size

  • A bit == 0 or 1
  • 8 bits == 1 byte
  • 2^10 bytes == 1 KB (non-CS people approximate this by saying that it is 1,000 bytes)
  • 2^20 bytes == 1 MB (non-CS people approximate this by saying that it is 1,000,000 bytes)
  • 2^30 bytes == 1 GB (non-CS people approximate this by saying that it is 1,000,000,000 bytes)
  • 2^40 bytes == 1 TB (non-CS people approximate this by saying that it is 1,000,000,000,000 bytes)

Transmission rates

  • 1 Kbps == 1000 bits/sec
  • 1 KBps == 1000 bytes/sec

Big B for bytes, little b for bits.

Binary numbers

How do we assign meaning to binary data?

If we are dealing with text, one way is to use a binary number to represent a single character.

One common encoding scheme is ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange).

In this scheme, the letter 'a' is represented by the binary number 01100001.

All ASCII characters are represented by 7 bits, which means that there are 128 possible characters that can be represented.

  • 97 = 'a'
  • 97 decimal == 01100001
Check yourself

what is the smallest 7 bit number?

A number with all 0's is the smallest 7 bit number. Bit 1: 0 * 1 == 0 Bit 2: 0 * 2 == 0 Bit 3: 0 * 4 == 0 Bit 4: 0 * 8 == 0 Bit 5: 0 * 16 == 0 Bit 6: 0 * 32 == 0 Bit 7: 0 * 64 == 0

Check yourself

what is the largest 7 bit number?

A number with all 1's is the largest 7 bit number. Bit 1: 1 * 1 == 1 Bit 2: 1 * 2 == 2 Bit 3: 1 * 4 == 4 Bit 4: 1 * 8 == 8 Bit 5: 1 * 16 == 16 Bit 6: 1 * 32 == 32 Bit 7: 1 * 64 == 64

1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 + 32 + 64 == 127

Check yourself

Including 0, how many values are in this range?

If you include 0 which is a valid number and count all the way up to 127 there are 128 different values

There are other encoding schemes like UTF-8 that can represent many more characters than ASCII.

UTF-8 uses between 1 and 4 bytes to represent a character.

If the first bit is 0, then the character is represented by 1 byte (using 0-127 of the seven remaining bits).

00000000 == 0 
...
...
0|0110000 == 48 '0'
0|0110001 == 49 '1'
...
0|0111001 == 57 '9'
...
0|1000001 == 65 'A'
0|1000010 == 66 'B'
0|1011010 == 90 'Z'
...
0|1100001 == 97 'a'
0|1100010 == 98 'b'
0|1100011 == 99 'c'
0|1111010 == 122 'z'
...
...
01111111 == 127

If the first bit is 1, then the character is represented by multiple bytes. The number of bytes is determined by the number of leading 1s in the first byte.

For example, if the first byte starts with 110, then the character is represented by 2 bytes. All continuation bytes start with 10.

2 bytes
110|00011 10|101001 == 'é'

If the first byte starts with 1110, then the character is represented by 3 bytes.

3 bytes
1110|0010 10|000010 10|101100 == '€'

If the first byte starts with 11110, then the character is represented by 4 bytes.

4 bytes
11110|000 10|011111 10|011000 10|000000 == '😀'

Character data is one way to translate data to information but some organizations and software systems create their own meaning for the bits that make up our info.

Here is an example of a MS Word document opened up in my text editor.

When I view the MS Word document in my text editor, it is treating each of the bytes in the file as if they were UTF-8 characters.

However, this is not how the MS Word application interprets the bytes in the file.

The MS Word application has its own meaning for the bytes in the file.

Transmitting Bytes

Another issue is the order that bytes get sent across the network.

If I have a 4 byte integer:

01001101011000010111001001101011b == 1,298,231,915d

The question is, in what order do we send the bytes across the network?

01001101 01100001 01110010 01101011

The answer is that it depends on the protocol that the machines are using to communicate!

  • Big Endian- the most significant byte is sent first
  • Little Endian- the least significant byte is sent first

The communicating machines have to agree on which order to use.
